children: NSE’s dominance gives it a significant competitive moat, but it also means regulatory changes to derivatives markets can have an outsized impact on its earnings

The National Stock Exchange of India’s (NSE) much-awaited public-market debut has brought its market dominance, valuation and earnings model under closer investor scrutiny. Despite commanding an overwhelming share of India’s equity trading and attracting strong demand for its Rs 22,569 crore initial public offering (IPO), NSE’s shares made only a modest debut, highlighting the challenge of translating a dominant franchise into sustained public-market returns.

NSE shares opened at Rs 1,800 on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) on 24 September, just 0.9 per cent above the issue price of Rs 1,785, before touching Rs 1,840 during the session. The muted debut came despite a 5.71-times subscribed Rs 22,569 crore IPO, strong institutional demand and years of interest in NSE shares in the unlisted market.

Market participants say the subdued start should not be read as a verdict on NSE’s business franchise. Instead, it highlights the transition from an unlisted asset, where scarcity supported investor interest, to a public company whose valuation will now be tested every day against earnings, competition, regulation and future share supply.
From Scarcity Premium To Public-market Scrutiny

The sheer scale of NSE’s franchise is difficult to overlook. The exchange accounted for 92.99 per cent of India’s cash-market share and 99.79 per cent of equity futures in financial year 2026. It also held a 74.71 per cent share of equity options by premium turnover during the year.
Yet the IPO valuation left relatively limited room for a sharp listing gain, according to market participants.

“At around 47 times earnings the pricing was full, with limited room for a listing pop,” said Ratiraj Tibrewal, Director, Choice Capital Advisors. “NSE is a strong business priced close to fair value, and a quiet start is what that usually looks like.”

Tibrewal said the experience of previous large IPOs suggests issue size alone does not determine post-listing performance. Pricing and the supply of shares after listing can be more important factors.

“The other pattern is supply. Large issues usually have a big pool of existing holders waiting to sell once lock-ins end, and that caps the upside for months,” he said. “A muted listing on its own says very little. What happens over the next year depends on earnings, not day one.”

The NSE IPO was entirely an offer for sale (OFS), with 12.64 crore shares sold by existing shareholders. No fresh capital was raised by the exchange, meaning the proceeds accrued to selling shareholders rather than being deployed into the business.
This distinction could become increasingly important as investors begin valuing NSE on its own earnings trajectory rather than the scarcity value attached to its unlisted shares.
The Derivatives Question

The biggest fundamental issue for NSE is its dependence on transaction-led income, particularly derivatives. Transaction charges accounted for 78.65 per cent of NSE’s revenue from operations in FY26, while options contributed 60.22 per cent. This concentration makes the exchange highly sensitive to changes in trading activity, taxation and market structure.

“Key risks include tighter F&O regulations, higher trading costs and taxes, changes in retail participation, and structural changes such as the Closing Auction Session,” said Hemang Gor, Senior Research Analyst, Derivatives & Technical Research, Axis Direct.

Gor pointed to the sharp decline in overall traded contracts as evidence of the sensitivity of NSE’s earnings to derivatives activity. Total traded contracts fell from 103.3 billion in FY25 to 37 billion in FY26, a 64.2 per cent contraction.

“I expect F&O volumes to settle at a lower but more sustainable baseline compared with the pandemic-era boom,” he said. “Regulatory measures and higher capital requirements are likely to reduce speculative retail activity, while institutional participation should become relatively more important.”

That creates a more complicated growth equation for NSE. A structurally expanding Indian capital market can support the exchange over the long term, but the volume boom that powered derivatives activity in recent years may not be repeated in the same form.

Gor expects activity to increasingly shift towards monthly expiries, hedging and defined-risk strategies rather than high-frequency expiry-day speculation. That could mean lower transaction revenue in the near term, but potentially a more mature derivatives ecosystem over time.
Regulatory
Risk
NSE’s dominance gives it a significant competitive moat, but it also means regulatory changes to derivatives markets can have an outsized impact on its earnings.

Tibrewal said investors would need to track whether derivatives volumes remain resilient after the increase in securities transaction tax (STT) and whether NSE can arrest the loss of share in index options.
“First, whether derivatives volumes hold up after the STT increase, and whether NSE can stop losing index options share. That line is 60 per cent of revenue,” he said.
“The regulatory direction” is the second key variable, he added, noting that further changes to derivatives regulations could immediately affect investor sentiment.

The challenge is particularly relevant because NSE’s market share in equity options by premium turnover had already moderated to 68.48 per cent in the first quarter of FY27 from 74.71 per cent in FY26.
This does not necessarily undermine the broader NSE franchise, but it does show that its dominant position cannot simply be assumed to translate into uninterrupted earnings growth.
BSE Comparison Becomes More Relevant

The listing also changes the way investors can compare India’s two major exchanges. At the NSE IPO price, the exchange was valued at around Rs 4.4 lakh crore. Shivani Nyati, Head of Wealth, Swastika Investmart, noted that NSE was valued at around 40.9-42.9 times FY26 diluted earnings per share at the issue price band, compared with around 54.3 times for BSE.

“NSE benefits from an expansive competitive moat and strong cash flow generation,” Nyati said, adding that the valuation discount to BSE could provide room for a long-term re-rating as India’s financialisation deepens.

However, she also highlighted the other side of the equation: around 79 per cent of NSE’s revenue remains linked to market trading volumes, leaving earnings exposed to market cycles and regulatory changes.
The public listing therefore gives investors something they did not previously have at the same scale: a continuously traded market benchmark against which NSE’s valuation can be assessed.
When IPO Hype Settles
For Sarvam Goel, Founder, Pocketful, the muted debut was more a reflection of pricing, market conditions and supply dynamics than a sign of weakness in NSE’s franchise.
“The subdued listing, in our view, was more a function of broader market sentiment and supply dynamics than NSE’s underlying fundamentals,” Goel said.
“The long-term investment case remains linked to the continued expansion of India’s capital markets and NSE’s dominant position within them,” he added.
But the next phase will be less about the novelty of owning NSE shares and more about whether the exchange can convert its market position into sustainable earnings growth.
Tibrewal also flagged a potential supply overhang when pre-IPO shareholders become eligible to sell from around March 2027. “That is a real supply overhang,” he said.
At the same time, he expects the absence of a one-time Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) settlement charge that affected FY26 profit to make subsequent quarterly earnings appear stronger.

For investors, that leaves NSE with an unusual combination of advantages and questions. It has overwhelming market share, strong cash generation and exposure to India’s expanding financial markets. But its valuation already reflects much of that franchise strength, while derivatives remain central to its revenue and regulation can materially alter trading behaviour.

The first day of trading has therefore provided little evidence either way. The more important test will be whether NSE can sustain its dominance, diversify its revenue base and deliver earnings growth sufficient to justify its public-market valuation as the scarcity premium of the unlisted market disappears.
Krishna Chourasia
